Treatment of enterococcal endocarditis is based on combinations of an aminogly- coside with another antibacterial, usually a beta lactam or a glycopeptide, depending on the sensitivity of the isolated organism. For gentamicin sensitive, penicillin sensitive enterococ- ci: intravenous bolus injections of ampicillin or amoxi- cillin 2 g (or benzylpenicillin 2.4 g) every 4 hours and gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 or 12 hours, both given for at least 4 weeks.4,6,8 If the patient is allergic to penicillin, or the isolate is penicillin resistant but gentamicin sensitive, then a com- bination of vancomycin or teicoplanin with gentamicin may be given for at least 4 weeks.6-8 For enterococci with high level gentamicin resistance, a penicillin as above may be used with streptomycin 7.5 mg/kg twice daily (intramuscularly or intravenous- ly) for at least 4 weeks.6,8 If there is also penicillin resist- ance, or the patient is penicillin allergic, streptomycin as above may be given with vancomycin or teicoplanin.6 If streptomycin cannot be used then treatment should be given for at least 8 weeks.6 Endocarditis due to multiply resistant enterococci not susceptible to penicillin, gentamicin, or vancomycin, is still infrequent and there seem to be no established reg- imens; options may include the use of linezolid or quin- upristin/dalfopristin where available.6,8 A combination of ampicillin with ceftriaxone or imipenem-cilastatin, given for at least 8 weeks, has been suggested for multi- ply resistant E. faecalis infection in US guidelines.8 • HACEK endocarditis. The HACEK organisms are slow and difficult to culture and treatment must often, therefore, be empirical. Traditionally, treatment for this group of organisms was based on ampicillin and gen- tamicin. However, because of the emergence of beta- lactamase producing strains, empirical treatment is now based on beta-lactamase-stable cephalosporins.
